entries.topicDescription: The imperative UI framework that underpins most production iOS apps.

tips.title: Auto Layout with anchors is the modern way
tips.content:
Auto Layout defines your UI with constraints rather than fixed
frames. The system calculates positions and sizes at runtime,
adapting to different screen sizes and orientations.

The anchor API (NSLayoutConstraint anchors) is the cleanest
way to create constraints in code. Each view has anchors for
top, bottom, leading, trailing, width, height, and center.

Always set translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints to false
when creating views in code. Forgetting this is the number
one Auto Layout mistake — your constraints will conflict with
auto-generated ones.

Activate constraints in batches with NSLayoutConstraint.activate
for better performance.

tips.title: Diffable data sources make collection views reliable
tips.content:
UICollectionViewDiffableDataSource (iOS 13+) replaces the
old numberOfItemsInSection/cellForItemAt pattern with a
snapshot-based approach.

You create a snapshot describing the current state of your
data, then apply it. The framework automatically calculates
insertions, deletions, and moves with smooth animations.

No more "Invalid number of items" crashes from mismatched
data source counts. The snapshot is the single source of
truth, and you apply it atomically.

Combine this with compositional layouts for complex,
multi-section collection views that are still easy to reason
about and maintain.

tips.title: Coordinator pattern bridges UIKit and SwiftUI
tips.content:
UIViewControllerRepresentable lets you wrap any UIKit view
controller for use in SwiftUI. The key is the Coordinator — a
class that acts as delegate and data source.

The coordinator lives between SwiftUI's value-type world and
UIKit's reference-type world. It handles delegate callbacks
and communicates changes back via bindings.

Create the coordinator in makeCoordinator(), set it as the
delegate in makeUIViewController(), and update state in
updateUIViewController(). This three-step pattern covers
virtually any UIKit integration.

This is essential for using UIKit components that have no
SwiftUI equivalent: camera, map annotations, PDF views, etc.
